strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss early enough to guide hyperparameter selection directly on the target model.

The position-dependent hyperbolic representation is interpretable and supported by strong empirical fits across checkpoints and model sizes. Additional GPT-NeoX and MoE experiments broaden the evidence beyond one architecture.

The forecasting experiments go beyond retrospective fitting: they extrapolate from 10–40% of training on 468M, 1.2B, and 6.7B models, with substantial reported improvements over three baselines on both ID and OOD validation data. The reported R² of 0.87 for the 1.2B model using 10% of training is encouraging.

The data-mixture application evaluates selected models after completing training, reporting lower perplexity in all four comparisons and improvements in 12 of 14 downstream benchmark comparisons. Equations, architecture tables, and pseudocode communicate the broad procedure clearly.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the benefit of token-position modeling. The proposed method uses a piecewise log-log/cosine forecast with knowledge of the training schedule, whereas the aggregate-loss baselines use simpler functional families. After freezing a0 and a1, the proposed aggregate loss is itself a constant plus a2(N). An aggregate-loss baseline using the same functional family and schedule information, together with component ablations, is needed to establish what drives the gains.

Important reproducibility details remain unresolved. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, applies calibration when Npred ≤ Nsep, contradicting Section 2.4, which requires observations after the separation point. Outlier rejection thresholds, fitting initialization and constraints, evaluation frequency, and exact mixture candidates are unspecified. The manuscript provides no implementation or loss-trace release to resolve these ambiguities. These gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation despite the promising results.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence is limited at the actual operating budget. Selection uses 10B tokens, only 2.5% of the 400B training budget, while forecasting evaluations begin at 10%. Predicted versus realized final losses and rankings for all five candidates are not reported. Perplexity gains are approximately 0.7–1.3%, without uncertainty estimates; averaging five neighboring checkpoints does not measure independent-run variability. The total search cost is also insufficiently documented.

The claimed generality exceeds the forecasting evidence. Training uses the Pile, one tokenizer, and cosine schedules, and the forecast explicitly incorporates that schedule. Additional architectures and evaluation datasets primarily demonstrate retrospective fits. The conclusions should be scoped to these conditions, or supported by forecasting tests under different schedules and training distributions.

The theoretical interpretations need correction. Appendix C rejects exponential functions because they approach zero after setting their additive offset to zero, although the stated exponential family permits a positive asymptote. Equation 17 follows from imposing constant a0 and a1; equal observed loss reductions do not establish that position weighting is unnecessary. The three suppression experiments support only a limited empirical finding about those particular weighting choices.

The novelty framing overlooks prior training-step scaling and learning-curve extrapolation. Kaplan et al. already consider loss dependence on training steps, so describing temporal modeling as previously unexplored is too broad. The contribution should be positioned around the particular positional decomposition and forecasting construction, with comparisons to relevant extrapolation methods.
